reception.text: A syndicated item treated the strip as a curiosity, "NOVEL RESERVATION," and misreported its width as thirty feet.
No comment for or against has been found in the California and Washington papers searched.
reception.source: California Digital Newspaper Collection; Washington Digital Newspapers, June–August 1908

political_impact.text: The proclamation answered a 1907 United States proposal for a joint sixty-foot strip on the Alaska–Yukon line, extended to the whole frontier in line with Canada's wishes.
political_impact.source: International Boundary Commission, Joint Report (1918), pp. 20–22

political_impact.text: Because the text contemplated patents to land on the strip, new claims could still be started and carried to patent with only a recital.

legacy.text: The northern strip remains one of the least-known of Roosevelt's reservations, resting today as much on Taft's 1912 proclamation as on Roosevelt's.

today.name: Sixty-foot federal strip along the Canadian border
today.note: Reissued in stronger terms by Taft's Proclamation 1196 (1912).

related.note: The Mexican-border strip of 1907, of which this is the northern counterpart, though worded differently.

later_actions.text: Taft's Proclamation 1196 reserved the strip from all entry and disposition under the public-land laws, protecting claims made before June 15, 1908 and letting those made between 1908 and 1912 go to patent subject to the reservation.

uncertain: Which United States department first proposed the Alaska strip in October 1907 is not known; State Department files (NARA RG 59) would settle it.
Which agency administers the northern strip today, and whether any of it has been transferred, is not known.
Why Taft reissued the reservation in 1912 is not stated.
Reception in Montana, North Dakota, Minnesota and Maine papers has not been searched.
